title: 𒉆𒈗
titleEn: Sumerian King List — Kish, the first dynasty after the Flood (I 42 – II 46)
part: Kish, the first dynasty after the Flood (I 42 – II 46)
draftNote: Draft — the cuneiform and its readings are provisional, checked sign-by-sign against Langdon's 1923 edition of the prism.
source: Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444), after S. Langdon, Oxford Editions of Cuneiform Texts II (Oxford, 1923), I 42 – II 46. Cuneiform in normalized Unicode (Neo-Assyrian forms) though the prism is Old Babylonian. Academic transliteration in modern subscript notation over Langdon's 1923 readings; Langdon's restorations shown in [ ] and his superseded readings flagged in the notes; pronunciation conventional reconstructed Sumerian. Fresh translations from the Sumerian; Langdon's public-domain translation consulted for sense only.
about: After the Flood kingship comes down again, to Kish: twenty-three kings, from Ĝa-ur to Agga, among them Etana the shepherd who went up to heaven. Four lines at the top of Col. II are lost and two more are only begun, so some names are gone. The reigns are still enormous but shrinking — hundreds of years now, not tens of thousands — and the dynasty's total does not match the reigns that survive; the notes say so rather than correct it. Readings follow Langdon's 1923 edition, signs as his copy of the prism shows them; several names, a few signs and the grammar of one line are uncertain, and the notes flag each case.

sentences.t: 𒆧𒆠 𒉆𒈗𒆷

morph.gloss: Kish — city in northern Babylonia, seat of the first dynasty after the Flood (KIŠ + place-det ki)

sentences.i: the kingship was in Kish.
sentences.n: The second beginning: after the Flood (I 39–41) the list opens again at Kish, below a ruled line. The pattern is the one the list used for Eridu (I 2): the city, then nam-lugal-la, 'the kingship'. KI after KIŠ is the place-determinative, not read aloud. -la is the vowel ending -a written after the l of lugal; the grammar books disagree on its exact force (locative 'in' or a genitive), but the sense is that Kish now held the kingship.

sentences.i: In Kish, Ĝa-ur became king; he reigned 1,200 years.
sentences.n: Three prism lines make the first reign: the city, the king's name, lugal-am₃ 'was king' (copula -am₃ written a-an), then the reign formula. Kish has no case-ending: 'in' is understood, as in the antediluvian list. The name is Langdon's Gà-ur — the GA₂ sign (his 'MAL') followed by UR, read ĝa₂-ur here; how the name was really pronounced is uncertain. On the prism a wide space separates Kish from the name; Langdon (fn. 5) asks whether a small sign was lost there, sees no traces, and believes nothing is missing. The number is two geš'u signs, 2 × 600 = 1,200.

sentences.i: Gulla-Nidaba-anna[…]el reigned 960 years.
sentences.n: A royal name, partly damaged. The prism shows GUL-LA, the divine determinative (AN, unread), the sign of the grain-goddess Nidaba (Nisaba, written NAGA), AN-NA, then a broken stretch, and EL at the end of the line. The broken stretch is shown as a gap; Langdon leaves it unread. He adds (fn. 6) that Gulla-ezen-an-na… is also a possible reading — that is, the fourth sign is not certain. The number is written geš'u + 6 geš: 600 + 360 = 960.
The top of Col. II is broken away: four lines are lost entirely. Langdon (fn. 2) judges that they held two royal names with their reigns, corresponding to Poebel's Nippur fragment No. 5, I 1–3.
Lost line (see II 1).
Lost line (see II 1).
Lost line — the last of the four. Langdon's translation of it reads only '… reigned ? years.'

sentences.n: Only the first sign, BA, survives; the rest of the line is broken. Langdon restores Ba[ba?-gul-?e? mu ? ni-ag], with his own question marks throughout (and a Nippur parallel, Poebel No. 5 I 4). That restoration is too uncertain to show as signs, so only BA and a gap are given: a king whose name began Ba-, and his reign.

sentences.i: Galibum reigned 960 years.
sentences.n: The first fully preserved name of the column. li₂ is the NI sign (Langdon lí). The name looks Semitic (Akkadian-type -um ending) — from here on several Kish names do. Langdon notes the same king on three Nippur duplicates. 960 = geš'u + 6 geš.

sentences.i: Kalumu reigned 840 years.
sentences.n: Name and reign on one line. Langdon reads Ka-lu-mu-mu mu, which needs three MU signs; his own copy on Plate I shows only two (KA-LU-MU-MU, then the number). Here the second MU is taken as 'years' and the name as Ka-lu-mu; a final -um may simply be unwritten. The Nippur copies have Ga-lu-mu-um, Ka-lu-mu-um and Ga-lu-mu-um-e (Langdon fn. 6), which support a name Kalumum. 840 = geš'u + 4 geš.

sentences.i: Duggagib reigned 900 years.
sentences.n: The first sign is KA, which can be read dug₄ ('speak') or zu₂ ('tooth'). Langdon (fn. 7) reads dúg = dug₄; Poebel had read zu-ga-gi-ib-(e), which Langdon rejects together with the 'Scorpion King' interpretation built on it. The reading of the name is therefore uncertain. gi₄ is Langdon's gí. 900 = geš'u + 5 geš.

maš-da — Langdon 'a poor man' (written BAR-DA, not the usual MAŠ); sense in the list uncertain

sentences.i: Arpium, son of a poor man (?), reigned 720 years.
sentences.n: The first king given a father. dumu 'son' + maš-da + -ke₄ (Langdon -ge): genitive 'of' plus the ergative -e, because 'the son of …' is the subject of the reign verb. Langdon (fn. 10) notes that the sign here is BAR, not the usual MAŠ, and translates maš-da as 'a poor man'; the sense of this word in the list is uncertain, and 'a poor man' in the English is his, marked (?). The second sign, Langdon's dā (with a macron), is drawn on his copy like the NI of ni-ag in the next line, not like the DA of ma-da in II 36; it is shown as DA after his reading, but the sign is uncertain. u₂ is Langdon's ú. Nippur variants of the name: Ar-pi-i, Ar-pu-um, Ar-pi-ú (fn. 9); there the order of these six kings is Galibum, Atab, Atabba, Kalumum, Duggagib, Arpium (fn. 11). 720 = geš'u + 2 geš.

sentences.i: Etana, the shepherd, the one who went up to heaven, who made all the foreign lands firm, became king; he reigned 1,500 years.
sentences.n: The longest entry so far, four prism lines. sipa 'shepherd' is PA + LU (Langdon sib), a royal title. lu₂ 'man' introduces 'the one who …' twice. an-še₃: an 'heaven' + terminative -še₃ 'to' (the EŠ₂ sign; Langdon -šú). ba-e₃-de₃ (Langdon ba-ĕ-dé): e₃, written UD.DU, is the verb 'go out / go up', and the final de₃ (NE) is read with it, as in the opening line of the list (e₃-de₃-a-ba); the Nippur copies write ba-e₃-da and ni-ib-e₃-da (fn. 12), with the -a that makes a 'who' clause. kur-kur is 'mountain-land' doubled: all the foreign lands. mu-un-gi-na: gi-n 'make firm, establish' with the prefix chain mu-n- and the -a of the 'who' clause (Langdon: 'made the foreign lands faithful'). Etana's ascent is the subject of a well-known Babylonian legend. 1,500 = 2 geš'u + 5 geš; a Nippur copy has 600 + 35 (?) (fn. 13).

sentences.n: iz is the GIŠ sign; kar₃ is Langdon's kàr — the third sign is read GAN here after Langdon's value, but its identification on the copy is not certain. The number is unusual: instead of geš signs the scribe writes 5 šu-ši + 6 — 'five sixties and six', with šu-ši 'sixty' spelled out as a word (Akkadian šūši). 5 × 60 + 6 = 306.

sentences.i: Ilku reigned 900 years.
sentences.n: Langdon reads Il-ku-u ('Ilkû'); on his copy the third sign is not the single corner-wedge U but a larger sign, taken here as U₃ (ù) — an uncertain identification. A Nippur copy may have Il-ku-u-um (fn. 1). The number: Langdon reads 600 + 300 = 900, but notes (fn. 2) that it is 'written 60 + 15! by wrong spacing of the figures'. On the copy the upright wedge of the geš'u stands apart from its corner-wedge, so the group looks like 1 (= 60) + 10 + 5. Read as geš'u + 5 geš it is 900, which is what is shown.

sentences.i: Enmenbaragigur, the man who made the weapons of the land of Elam bow down, became king; he reigned 900 years.
sentences.n: Four prism lines. The name is Langdon's En-me-en-bara-gi-gur; the king is better known today as Enmebaragesi, with the last signs read differently. lu₂ 'the man who …'. ma-da 'land'; elam{ki}-ma: Elam (the NIM sign + ki) + the genitive -a(k) 'of', written -ma after m. {ĝeš}tukul 'weapon' is the KU sign with the wood-determinative GIŠ (Langdon ᵍⁱˢku). -bi 'its': read with Elam — 'its (Elam's) weapons' — the phrase is the object of the verb. ib-ta-an-gam: gam 'bend, bow down' with the prefix chain ib-ta-n-; Langdon (fn. 3) takes -ta- as an instrumental infix and translates 'with his weapon subdued' the land of Elam. Both readings are possible; the grammar of the line is debated. A Nippur copy has this line (P. No. 3 II 1). 900 = geš'u + 5 geš; the same copy has 600 + 300 (?) (fn. 4).

sentences.i: Agga, son of Enmenbaragigur, reigned 625 years.
sentences.n: The last king of the dynasty: AK + GA, Langdon's Ag-ga (also cited as Aka). He is the Agga of Kish known from the Sumerian story of his conflict with Gilgamesh of Uruk. A Nippur copy has Ag dumu En-me-bara… (fn. 5). -ke₄: 'son of …' as subject. 625 = geš'u + 2 u + 5 — the same figure as the Nippur copy (fn. 6).

sentences.l: 23 kings; their-years 24510, months 3, days 3 (and) half-a-day they-ruled.

morph.gloss: half a day (u₄ 'day' + maš 'half', written with BAR)

sentences.i: Twenty-three kings reigned 24,510 years, 3 months and 3½ days.
sentences.n: The dynasty's total, over three lines. mu-bi 'its/their years'; ib-ag (modern íb-aĝ₂) is the reign verb of the totals, rendered 'they ruled': its -b- is not a plural ending (it is the third-person marker of the non-personal class), so the plural English follows the sense. 24,510 is written 6 šar₂ + 4 geš'u + 8 geš + 3 u (21,600 + 2,400 + 480 + 30); on the copy the šar₂ cluster cannot be counted with complete certainty, but these counts give Langdon's figure. iti 'month' (Langdon ita), then u₄ 'day' (Langdon ud) 3 and u₄-maš, a half-day (maš 'half', again the BAR sign, as in II 14). The total does not add up: Langdon (fn. 8) says the 19 preserved reigns come to 12,491 and that the scribe's total 'cannot be correct'. His 12,491 does not match the figures he himself prints: the nineteen reigns as this copy writes them (and as Langdon transliterates them) add up to 15,751 — still far short of 24,510. The months and days are a strange precision for a list of giant reigns. A Nippur copy inserts a sub-total for Enmenbaragigur and his son (fn. 7).

ba-ĝen — 'went, passed' (ĝen written with the DU sign)

sentences.i: Kish was smitten with weapons; its kingship was carried to Eanna.
sentences.n: The refrain that closes a historical dynasty: the city is defeated and the kingship moves. {ĝeš}tukul 'weapon(s)' has no case ending; the sense 'with weapons' is understood. ba-an-sig₃ (Langdon ba-an-sīg; he also prints it sig): sig₃ 'strike, smite', with the prefixes ba-an-; the -n- would ordinarily mark a 'he' who does the smiting, so the passive English ('was smitten') follows the sense of the refrain rather than every element of the form. On the copy the verb is one compact sign, taken here as PA.GAN₂ = sig₃; the identification of the drawn form is not certain. Eanna, 'House of Heaven', is the temple of Inanna at Uruk, standing here for the city whose kings come next. e₂ 'house' (Langdon é), an-na 'of heaven', -še₃ 'to' (Langdon -šú). ba-ĝen (Langdon ba-gín; the DU sign) 'went'. On the prism ba-ĝen is written below, in the same line (Langdon prints it on a second, unnumbered line).

glossary.-am₃: enclitic copula 'is / was' — written am₃ = a-an
glossary.-ke₄: genitive -ak 'of' + ergative -e, written with the KID sign (Langdon -ge) — marks a genitive phrase such as 'son of X' as the subject (agent) of the verb; not always written
glossary.-ma: genitive -a(k) 'of', written -ma after a final m (elam{ki}-ma 'of Elam')
glossary.[…]: a lost stretch of text — a gap where the signs are broken away on the prism
glossary.ag-ga: Agga (Langdon Ag-ga, also cited as Aka) — last king of the first dynasty of Kish, son of Enmenbaragigur; AK + GA; the Agga of the Sumerian story of his conflict with Gilgamesh of Uruk
glossary.ar-pi-u₂-um: Arpium — king of Kish, son of a maš-da (Langdon 'a poor man'); u₂ is Langdon's ú; Nippur copies vary the name (Ar-pi-i, Ar-pu-um, Ar-pi-ú)
glossary.a₂-tab: Atab — king of Kish; a₂ is the A₂ sign ('arm'), tab the TAB sign ('double'); as a name its meaning is not clear
glossary.a₂-tab-ba: Atabba — king of Kish, following Atab; the added -ba makes a distinct name
glossary.ba-: ba- — verbal prefix (often of motion away, or a middle/passive sense)
glossary.ba-[…]: a royal name beginning Ba-, the rest lost; only the BA sign survives (Langdon restores Ba[ba?-gul-?e?] with his own question marks, too uncertain to show)
glossary.ba-an-: ba-n- — verbal prefix chain: ba- (often of motion away, or a middle/passive sense) + -n-, which ordinarily marks a 'he' who acts
glossary.ba-gín: ba-ĝen — 'went, passed' (ĝen written with the DU sign)
glossary.ba-li-iḫ: Balih — king of Kish, son of Etana; iḫ is the AḪ sign; a Nippur copy spells the name Wa-li-iḫ
glossary.bar-sal-nun-na: Barsalnunna — king of Kish, a second son of Enmenunna; father of Tupzah; a Nippur copy omits 'son of Enmenunna'
glossary.bu-[…]: a royal name beginning Bu-, followed by the divine determinative, so a god's name; the rest lost (Langdon restores Bu-ᵈ[En-zu], 'Bu-Sin (?)', after a Nippur fragment, with question marks)
glossary.dug₄-ga-gi₄-ib: Duggagib (Langdon Dúg-ga-gí-ib) — king of Kish; first sign KA, readable dug₄ 'speak' or zu₂ 'tooth'; Langdon reads dug₄ and rejects Poebel's zu-ga-gi-ib, so the name's reading is uncertain
glossary.dumu: son, child — written with the TUR sign, read dumu; 'dumu X' = 'son of X'
glossary.e-ta-na: Etana — king of Kish, 'the shepherd who went up to heaven, who made all the foreign lands firm'; his ascent is the subject of a well-known Babylonian legend; father of Balih
glossary.elam: Elam — land east of Babylonia; written with the NIM sign plus place-determinative ki, as elam{ki}
glossary.en-me-en-bara₂-gi-gur: Enmenbaragigur (Langdon En-me-en-bara-gi-gur) — king of Kish, 'the man who made the weapons of the land of Elam bow down'; better known today as Enmebaragesi, the last signs being read differently; father of Agga
glossary.en-me-nun-na: Enmenunna — king of Kish; en 'lord' + me + nun 'prince' + -na, a name of the same shape as the En-men-… kings before the Flood; father of Melam-Kish and Barsalnunna
glossary.e₂-an-na: Eanna, 'House of Heaven' — Inanna's temple at Uruk (Langdon É-an-na); e₂ 'house' + an-na 'of heaven'
glossary.e₃: to descend (verb e₃) · to go out, go up (also written UD.DU; Langdon ĕ)
glossary.ga-li₂-bu-um: Galibum — king of Kish; li₂ is the NI sign (Langdon lí); the name looks Semitic (Akkadian-type -um ending); Langdon notes the same king on three Nippur duplicates
glossary.gam: to bend, bow down; (with -n-) to make bow down, subdue
glossary.gi-n: to make firm, establish — gi-n 'firm, true'; Langdon 'make faithful'
glossary.gul-la-{d}nidaba-an-na-[…]-el: Gulla-Nidaba-anna… — king of Kish, the second named in the dynasty; GUL-LA, divine determinative, the Nidaba (Nisaba, grain-goddess) sign NAGA, AN-NA, a broken stretch left unread, then EL; Langdon notes Gulla-ezen-an-na… as another possible reading, so the fourth sign is uncertain
glossary.ib-ta-an-: ib-ta-n- — verbal prefix chain with -ta- ('from / with'; Langdon takes it as an instrumental infix) and -n- 'he'; its analysis is debated
glossary.il-ku-u₃: Ilku (Langdon Il-ku-u, 'Ilkû') — king of Kish; third sign taken as U₃ (ù) though on his copy it is larger than the single corner-wedge U, so uncertain; a Nippur copy may have Il-ku-u-um
glossary.il-ta-sa-du-um: Iltasadum — king of Kish; another Semitic-looking name in -um
glossary.ka-lu-mu: Kalumu — king of Kish; Langdon reads Ka-lu-mu-mu, but his own copy shows only two MU signs, so the second MU is taken as 'years' and a final -um may simply be unwritten; Nippur copies (Ga-lu-mu-um, Ka-lu-mu-um) support Kalumum
glossary.kiš: Kish — city in northern Babylonia, seat of the first dynasty after the Flood; written with the KIŠ sign plus the place-determinative KI (unread), as kiš{ki}
glossary.kur-kur: the foreign lands, all the mountain lands — kur 'mountain, foreign land' doubled as a plural; Langdon renders 'foreign lands'
glossary.lu₂: man; 'the one who …' — introduces a relative ('who') clause; Langdon galu
glossary.maš-da: maš-da — Langdon 'a poor man' (written BAR-DA, the sign BAR rather than the usual MAŠ); the sense in the list is uncertain, and 'poor man' is Langdon's, marked (?); the second sign (Langdon dā) is drawn on his copy like NI, so its identification as DA is uncertain
glossary.me-lam-kiš: Melam-Kish — king of Kish, son of Enmenunna; me-lam 'awe-inspiring radiance' + the city name Kish (with its determinative); King's Chronicles read A-lam-kiš-šu, which Langdon calls a scribal error
glossary.mu-un-: mu-n- — verbal prefix chain: mu- + -n- 'he' (the doer)
glossary.ni-ag: ì-aĝ₂ (Langdon 'ni-ag') — 'he ruled', lit. 'measured out'; reign verb, 3sg
glossary.sig₃: to strike, smite — written as one compact sign taken as PA.GAN₂ (Langdon sīg, also printed sig); the identification of the drawn form is uncertain
glossary.sipa: shepherd — written PA + LU (Langdon sib); also a royal title
glossary.ti-iz-kar₃: Tizkar (Langdon Ti-iz-kàr) — king of Kish, son of Tupzah; iz is GIŠ; the third sign is read GAN after Langdon's value, but its identification on the copy is uncertain
glossary.tukul: weapon, mace — the KU sign with the wood determinative ĝeš (Langdon ᵍⁱˢku)
glossary.tup-za-aḫ: Tupzah (Langdon Tup-za-aḫ) — king of Kish, son of Barsalnunna; first sign is Langdon's KIŠIB ('not MES'), in Unicode the MES character; its value in the name is uncertain, so the name's real form is too
glossary.u₄-maš: half a day — u₄ 'day' + maš 'half', maš written with the BAR sign
glossary.{d}: divine determinative (diĝir) — marks the following name as a god
glossary.{ĝeš}: wood determinative (ĝeš, the GIŠ sign) — unread, marks a wooden object; Langdon writes it as a raised ᵍⁱˢ
glossary.ĝa₂-ur: Ĝa-ur (Langdon Gà-ur) — first king of Kish after the Flood; GA₂ (Langdon's 'MAL') + UR; how the name was really pronounced is uncertain
glossary.šar₂: šar₂ — 3,600 (60 × 60); the working unit for the reign-lengths
glossary.šu-ši: šu-ši — 'sixty', written out as a word (Akkadian šūši) instead of with a numeral sign
